title: Question 1 – Acute abdominal pain with incomplete information
vignette: 22-year-old male presents with abdominal discomfort and a temperature of 38.2°C. Pain location, onset, radiation, and severity are unspecified.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Appendicitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Most common acute surgical abdomen in young males.

top5Differentials.name: Mesenteric Adenitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Frequent mimic of appendicitis in young adults.

top5Differentials.name: Meckel's Diverticulitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Prone to perforation and lower GI hemorrhage.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Nephrolithiasis with Pyelonephritis
top5Differentials.rationale: Obstructive uropathy with superimposed infection.

top5Differentials.name: Perforated Viscus / Acute Peritonitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Free perforation requiring emergent exploratory laparotomy.

mustNotMissConditions: Testicular Torsion with referred abdominal pain (mandatory scrotal exam)
explicitMissingInformation: Pain quadrant localization (RLQ, RUQ, LLQ, LUQ, epigastric, or generalized)
Pain onset timing, tempo (sudden vs gradual), character, and radiation
Pain severity rating (1-10)
Scrotal/genitourinary examination (rule out testicular torsion)
Peritoneal signs (guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness)
Complete vital signs (BP, HR, RR, SpO2)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Only fever (+1) is known. Formal risk tiering blocked.
Missing RR, BP, and GCS. Cannot evaluate sepsis mortality risk.

recommendedWorkup.action: Physical examination including abdomen quadrants and testicular exam
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Localize pathology and exclude testicular torsion.

recommendedWorkup.action: CBC with differential, CMP, Lipase, Urinalysis, CRP
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Assess leukocytosis, renal/hepatic function, pancreatitis, and UTI.

recommendedWorkup.action: Abdominal Ultrasound or Contrast-Enhanced CT Abdomen/Pelvis
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Cross-sectional imaging once exam localizes pathology.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Female-specific diagnoses (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, PID) must be strictly suppressed for this male encounter.
Never assign a definitive single-organ diagnosis when quadrant localization is unprovided.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Strict NPO status and obtain peripheral IV access
Full vital signs acquisition and structured physical exam
Isotonic crystalloid resuscitation

strictContraindications: Do NOT administer blind empiric antibiotics or heavy sedatives before attending surgical physical examination.
escalationTriggers: Peritoneal signs on exam
Hemodynamic instability (tachycardia HR > 110, hypotension SBP < 90 mmHg)
Testicular asymmetry or scrotal tenderness

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Jerusalem Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Acute Appendicitis

title: Question 2 – Suspected appendicitis
vignette: 26-year-old female presents with 18 hours of abdominal pain initially around the umbilicus, now localized to the right lower quadrant. Temperature 38.5°C, HR 108 bpm, nausea, and rebound tenderness. WBC 16,200/µL.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Appendicitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Classic migratory periumbilical-to-RLQ pain with peritonitis, leukocytosis, and pyrexia.

top5Differentials.name: Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy
top5Differentials.rationale: Reproductive-age female with acute RLQ peritonism; life-threatening hemorrhagic emergency.

top5Differentials.name: Right Ovarian Torsion
top5Differentials.rationale: Acute ischemic adnexal emergency requiring detorsion within 6 hours.

top5Differentials.name: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease / TOA
top5Differentials.rationale: Ascending pelvic infection causing peritonitis and high leukocytosis.

top5Differentials.name: Ruptured Hemorrhagic Ovarian Cyst
top5Differentials.rationale: Hemoperitoneum and peritoneal irritation following cyst rupture.

explicitMissingInformation: Urine or serum beta-hCG (MANDATORY in all reproductive-age females)
LMP and sexual history
Blood pressure (assess for shock)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Score >= 7 indicates high probability of appendicitis; warrants surgical consultation.
Strong indication for surgical exploration.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Urine/Serum qualitative beta-hCG
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Rule out ectopic pregnancy prior to imaging or surgery.

recommendedWorkup.action: Pelvic & Transvaginal Ultrasound with Doppler, followed by CT if equivocal
recommendedWorkup.rationale: First-line imaging in young females.

contradictionsAndCaveats: High Alvarado score does NOT rule out gynecologic emergencies in females.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: STAT pregnancy test (beta-hCG)
Emergency General Surgery Consultation

strictContraindications: Do NOT perform CT without checking pregnancy status.
escalationTriggers: Positive beta-hCG with free fluid on POCUS -> Emergent OB/GYN OR

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Jerusalem Guidelines for Acute Appendicitis

title: Question 3 – Acute pancreatitis
vignette: 48-year-old male presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, persistent vomiting, HR 122 bpm, and BP 94/62 mmHg. Lipase is 1,250 U/L.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Pancreatitis (Moderately Severe / Severe)
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe epigastric pain with back radiation + lipase 1,250 U/L.

top5Differentials.name: Perforated Peptic Ulcer Disease
top5Differentials.rationale: Epigastric pain and shock; can cause secondary lipase elevation.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia
top5Differentials.rationale: Profound pain with vomiting, tachycardia, and early shock.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Aortic Dissection / Ruptured AAA
top5Differentials.rationale: Back-radiating pain with tachycardia and borderline hypotension.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Ascending Cholangitis / Choledocholithiasis
top5Differentials.rationale: Gallstone passage is the primary etiology of acute pancreatitis.

mustNotMissConditions: Severe Acute Pancreatitis with persistent organ failure
explicitMissingInformation: BUN, Creatinine, Hematocrit (assess hemoconcentration and organ failure)
Respiratory rate and SpO2 (Marshall organ failure score)
Etiology clues (alcohol, gallstones, lipid panel)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Severe pain + lipase >= 3x ULN confirms pancreatitis. Early CT not needed on Day 1.
SIRS (HR 122) and age 48 present. Full score requires BUN and CXR.

recommendedWorkup.action: Transabdominal Right Upper Quadrant Ultrasound
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Detect gallstones and CBD dilation within 24 hours.

recommendedWorkup.action: CMP, CBC, Lactate, Triglycerides, Calcium
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Assess end-organ injury and etiology.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Do NOT order early contrast CT (< 48 hours) to evaluate necrosis: underestimates necrosis and IV contrast risks worsening AKI.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Aggressive Goal-Directed Fluid Resuscitation: Lactated Ringer's 5-10 mL/kg/h
Multimodal analgesia with IV opioids (Hydromorphone or Fentanyl)

strictContraindications: Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended in acute pancreatitis without documented infection.
escalationTriggers: Persistent organ failure > 48h (shock, Cr rise, PaO2/FiO2 < 300) -> ICU transfer

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Management of Acute Pancreatitis

title: Question 4 – Bowel obstruction versus perforation
vignette: 67-year-old female presents with abdominal distension, vomiting, constipation for four days, and severe generalized abdominal pain. HR 124 bpm, temperature 38.7°C. Lactate 4.8 mmol/L.

top5Differentials.name: Strangulated Closed-Loop Small Bowel Obstruction with Infarction
top5Differentials.rationale: Obstruction with SIRS and lactate 4.8 indicates bowel ischemia/strangulation.

top5Differentials.name: Perforated Viscus with Secondary Peritonitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe generalized peritonitis and lactic acidosis.

top5Differentials.name: Sigmoid or Cecal Volvulus with Gangrene
top5Differentials.rationale: Distension, absolute constipation, and high lactate.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia / Bowel Infarction
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe lactic acidosis and shock.

top5Differentials.name: Incarcerated / Strangulated Hernia
top5Differentials.rationale: Occult groin/femoral hernia causing closed-loop obstruction.

explicitMissingInformation: Blood pressure (assess for septic shock)
Physical exam peritoneal signs and groin exam for occult hernias

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Severe tissue hypoperfusion indicating high mortality.

recommendedWorkup.action: Upright Chest X-ray (free air) and Stat Contrast CT Abdomen/Pelvis
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Detect pneumoperitoneum and transition point.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Blood Cultures x2, CBC, CMP, Coags, Blood Gas
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Pre-op resuscitation and sepsis bundle.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Do NOT administer oral barium contrast: causes lethal chemical peritonitis if perforation is present.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: STAT General Surgery Consultation for Emergent Exploratory Laparotomy
Aggressive IV crystalloid (30 mL/kg) and NG tube decompression
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g IV)

strictContraindications: Do NOT delay surgery while awaiting imaging if peritonitis is overt.
escalationTriggers: Pneumoperitoneum, pneumatosis intestinalis, or refractory septic shock

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Management of Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction

title: Question 5 – Acute cholecystitis versus cholangitis
vignette: 62-year-old female presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever of 39.1°C, rigors, and jaundice. BP 102/68 mmHg, HR 112 bpm.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Ascending Cholangitis (Charcot's Triad)
top5Differentials.rationale: Classic Charcot triad (RUQ pain + high fever/rigors + jaundice) with SIRS.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Cholecystitis with Choledocholithiasis
top5Differentials.rationale: Gallbladder inflammation with secondary duct obstruction.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Suppurative Cholangitis / Reynolds Pentad
top5Differentials.rationale: Impending septic shock and central nervous system obtundation.

top5Differentials.name: Pyogenic Hepatic Abscess
top5Differentials.rationale: Hepatic parenchymal infection secondary to ascending biliary stasis.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Hepatitis / Fulminant Hepatic Failure
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe hepatocellular jaundice with fever.

mustNotMissConditions: Acute Ascending Cholangitis with septic shock
explicitMissingInformation: Mental status (screen for Reynolds Pentad)
Total & Direct Bilirubin, Alk Phos, AST, ALT
Lactate and coagulation profile

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Charcot triad fulfills TG18 criteria; requires urgent biliary decompression.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Transabdominal RUQ Ultrasound
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Confirm ductal dilation and choledocholithiasis.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Blood Cultures x2, CMP, Lactate, Coagulation Panel
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Confirm bacteremia, cholestasis, and coagulopathy.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Do NOT mistake cholangitis for simple cholecystitis: JAUNDICE indicates common bile duct obstruction and ascending bacterial sepsis!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: STAT Gastroenterology / IR Consultation for Emergent Biliary Decompression via ERCP (or PTBD)
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g IV)

strictContraindications: Do NOT perform elective cholecystectomy during acute cholangitis prior to biliary decompression.
escalationTriggers: Reynolds Pentad (hypotension or altered mental status) -> Emergent ERCP within hours

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: TG18 Guidelines for Management of Acute Cholangitis

title: Question 6 – Atypical myocardial infarction
vignette: 54-year-old male presents with nausea, fatigue, sweating, and mild epigastric discomfort without chest pain. ECG shows ST-segment depression in leads V4–V6. Troponin is elevated.

top5Differentials.name: Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI)
top5Differentials.rationale: Ischemic symptoms (diaphoresis, epigastric anginal equivalent) + ST depression + elevated troponin.

top5Differentials.name: Unstable Angina with High-Risk Features
top5Differentials.rationale: Subendocardial ischemia threatening progression to transmural infarction.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Peptic Ulcer Disease / Perforation
top5Differentials.rationale: Epigastric discomfort and nausea; can mimic or trigger cardiac events.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Aortic Dissection with Coronary Malperfusion
top5Differentials.rationale: Ascending dissection compromising coronary ostia, masquerading as ACS.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Pulmonary Embolism
top5Differentials.rationale: Right ventricular strain producing autonomic signs, diaphoresis, and troponin elevation.

mustNotMissConditions: Acute Aortic Dissection with Coronary Involvement
explicitMissingInformation: Exact quantitative Troponin delta at 1-2 hours
Blood pressure in bilateral arms and heart rate
Prior cardiac history (CAD, stents, CABG)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Mandates hospital admission and early invasive angiography within 24h.
High risk for death/MI; warrants early catheterization.

recommendedWorkup.action: Serial 12-lead ECGs q15-30 min and continuous ST-segment monitoring
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Detect dynamic progression to STEMI requiring immediate primary PCI.

recommendedWorkup.action: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin, CBC, CMP, Coagulation panel
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Quantify myocardial necrosis and baseline renal function prior to catheterization contrast.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Absence of chest pain does NOT rule out acute myocardial infarction: atypical presentations (nausea, diaphoresis, epigastric discomfort) are frequent in diabetics, elderly, and females.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Dual Antiplatelet Therapy: Aspirin 325 mg PO chewed immediately + P2Y12 inhibitor (Ticagrelor 180 mg)
Parenteral Anticoagulation: Therapeutic LMWH (Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC) or UFH
High-intensity statin (Atorvastatin 80 mg PO) and Cardiology consultation for early catheterization (< 24h)

strictContraindications: Fibrinolytic/thrombolytic therapy is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in NSTEMI (proven harm; only indicated in STEMI).
NSAIDs (except aspirin) are contraindicated in acute MI (increases myocardial rupture risk).
escalationTriggers: Dynamic ST-elevation on repeat ECG -> Immediate STEMI code activation for catheterization lab

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Guideline for Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain

title: Question 7 – Pulmonary embolism
vignette: 34-year-old female presents with sudden shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, HR 126 bpm, and oxygen saturation of 89%. She returned from a 12-hour flight two days ago.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Pulmonary Embolism (Submassive / Intermediate-High Risk)
top5Differentials.rationale: Sudden pleuritic pain, hypoxia (89%), severe tachycardia (126), and prolonged travel stasis.

top5Differentials.name: Spontaneous Pneumothorax
top5Differentials.rationale: Sudden pleuritic pain and hypoxemic dyspnea in young adult.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Pericarditis / Myopericarditis
top5Differentials.rationale: Pleuritic chest pain and sinus tachycardia.

top5Differentials.name: Community-Acquired Pneumonia with Pleurisy
top5Differentials.rationale: Pleurisy and hypoxemia, but sudden onset without fever favors vascular embolism.

top5Differentials.name: Aortic Dissection with Pleural Extension
top5Differentials.rationale: Sharp thoracic pain with tachycardia; vital to exclude prior to anticoagulation.

explicitMissingInformation: Blood pressure (distinguish Massive PE with shock SBP < 90 from Submassive PE)
Signs of Deep Vein Thrombosis on lower extremity exam
Bedside echocardiography RV strain findings

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: HR > 100 (+1.5), PE #1 diagnosis (+3.0), Recent travel/immobilization (+1.5). Mandates direct CTPA.
PERC CANNOT be used: Pre-test probability is not low; violates HR < 100 and SpO2 >= 95%.

recommendedWorkup.action: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Gold standard diagnostic imaging to confirm pulmonary arterial occlusion.

recommendedWorkup.action: Bedside Transthoracic Echocardiogram (POCUS)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Assess RV strain, McConnell sign, and rule out pericardial tamponade.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Do NOT order D-dimer in high-probability PE (Wells >= 6): negative D-dimer cannot safely exclude PE in high-risk patients. Proceed directly to CTPA.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Supplemental Oxygen to maintain SpO2 >= 92% and obtain IV access
Immediate Therapeutic Anticoagulation: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC or IV UFH bolus and infusion

strictContraindications: Do NOT delay anticoagulation for diagnostic imaging unless active major hemorrhage is present.
escalationTriggers: Hemodynamic collapse (sustained SBP < 90 mmHg -> Massive PE -> systemic thrombolysis)

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Acute Pulmonary Embolism

title: Question 8 – Aortic dissection
vignette: 61-year-old male with uncontrolled hypertension presents with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. BP is 190/110 mmHg in the right arm and 150/90 mmHg in the left arm.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Aortic Dissection (Stanford Type A vs Type B)
top5Differentials.rationale: Abrupt tearing pain radiating to back + 40 mmHg inter-arm pulse/pressure deficit (+LR > 10).

top5Differentials.name: Acute Coronary Syndrome / Inferior-Posterior STEMI
top5Differentials.rationale: Dissection can dissect retrogradely into right coronary ostium.

top5Differentials.name: Symptomatic Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Expansion / Impending Rupture
top5Differentials.rationale: Aneurysmal dilation with acute wall tension.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Pericarditis with Cardiac Tamponade
top5Differentials.rationale: Type A dissection leaking into pericardial space producing hemopericardium.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Pulmonary Embolism
top5Differentials.rationale: Sudden thoracic pain; lacks the inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy.

explicitMissingInformation: Heart rate and rhythm (target HR < 60 bpm in anti-impulse therapy)
Neurological exam (focal deficits from carotid involvement)
Peripheral pulse symmetry

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Tearing pain + pulse/BP discrepancy > 20 mmHg. Pre-test probability > 80%; mandates immediate CTA.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat CT Angiography (CTA) of the Chest, Abdomen, and Pelvis (Aorta protocol)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Classify Stanford Type A vs B and assess branch vessel perfusion.

recommendedWorkup.action: Bedside Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Evaluate ascending aortic root, pericardial effusion/tamponade, and acute aortic regurgitation.

contradictionsAndCaveats: NEVER administer pure vasodilators (Hydralazine, Sodium Nitroprusside) without PRIOR beta-blockade: reflex tachycardia increases shear stress (dP/dt), triggering catastrophic aortic rupture and propagation of the dissection flap!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: ANTI-IMPULSE THERAPY - STEP 1 (Beta-blockade): IV Esmolol infusion targeting HR < 60 bpm
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Eliminate ventricular ejection force and shear stress (dP/dt).

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: ANTI-IMPULSE THERAPY - STEP 2 (Vasodilator): IV Nicardipine added ONLY AFTER HR < 60 bpm, targeting SBP < 120 mmHg within 20 min
STAT Cardiothoracic and Vascular Surgery Consultation
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Immediate OR mobilization for Type A dissection.

strictContraindications: Vasodilators without prior beta-blockade are STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED.
Anticoagulation, antiplatelets, and thrombolytics are STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED (causes fatal hemorrhage into false lumen or pericardium).
escalationTriggers: Stanford Type A involvement -> Emergent open surgical repair STAT

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Guideline for Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease

title: Question 9 – Cardiogenic shock
vignette: 72-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease presents with chest pain, confusion, cold extremities, and hypotension. BP 78/48 mmHg, HR 130 bpm, lactate 5.2 mmol/L.

top5Differentials.name: Cardiogenic Shock secondary to Acute Myocardial Infarction
top5Differentials.rationale: CAD history, acute chest pain, profound hypotension (MAP 58), tachycardia, and high lactate (5.2).

top5Differentials.name: Mechanical Complication of Acute MI (Papillary Muscle Rupture / VSD)
top5Differentials.rationale: Abrupt hemodynamic collapse post-infarct due to acute mitral regurgitation or VSD.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Massive Pulmonary Embolism
top5Differentials.rationale: Obstructive cardiogenic shock from severe acute RV afterload.

top5Differentials.name: Cardiac Tamponade
top5Differentials.rationale: Obstructive shock with tachycardia, hypotension, and impaired filling.

top5Differentials.name: Distributive Septic Shock with Underlying CAD
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe lactic acidosis and encephalopathy; cold extremities favor cardiogenic hypoperfusion.

explicitMissingInformation: 12-Lead ECG findings (ST-elevation)
Bedside echocardiography findings (LVEF, wall motion, valve integrity)
Respiratory rate and SpO2 (pulmonary edema)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Profound hypotension, cold extremities, confusion, and lactate 5.2 mmol/L. Mortality > 40-50%; mandates emergent mechanical circulatory support and catheterization.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat 12-Lead ECG and Bedside Echocardiogram (POCUS)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Identify culprit STEMI and exclude mechanical rupture (VSD, papillary muscle rupture, tamponade).

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Troponin, Arterial Blood Gas, Lactate, CMP, CBC, Coagulation panel
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Quantify end-organ hypoperfusion.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Do NOT administer large fluid boluses in cardiogenic shock: volume loading in LV pump failure triggers catastrophic pulmonary edema and worsens oxygenation.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Vasopressor First-Line: Norepinephrine infusion (titrated to MAP >= 65 mmHg)
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Restore minimal coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Inotrope Addition: Dobutamine once MAP > 65 mmHg
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Augment myocardial contractility and stroke volume.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: STAT Cardiac Catheterization Lab Activation and Mechanical Circulatory Support (Impella / IABP / ECMO)

strictContraindications: Beta-blockers, CCBs, and ACE inhibitors are STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in cardiogenic shock.
escalationTriggers: Refractory hypotension -> Emergent Impella / VA-ECMO deployment

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Management of Cardiogenic Shock

title: Question 10 – Dangerous arrhythmia
vignette: 39-year-old male presents with palpitations, dizziness, and syncope. ECG shows a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 190 bpm.

top5Differentials.name: Ventricular Tachycardia (Monomorphic VT)
top5Differentials.rationale: Accounts for > 80% of regular wide-complex tachycardias; syncope and dizziness reflect severe hemodynamic compromise.

top5Differentials.name: Supraventricular Tachycardia with Aberrancy (SVT with BBB)
top5Differentials.rationale: Pre-existing bundle branch block with AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia.

top5Differentials.name: Antidromic Atrioventricular Re-entrant Tachycardia (WPW Syndrome)
top5Differentials.rationale: Antegrade conduction down accessory pathway; high risk of ventricular fibrillation if blocked incorrectly.

top5Differentials.name: Hyperkalemia-Induced Sine-Wave Wide Tachycardia
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe metabolic conduction block mimicking VT.

top5Differentials.name: Toxicological Sodium Channel Blocker Toxicity (TCA Overdose)
top5Differentials.rationale: Drug-induced QRS widening and rapid rate.

mustNotMissConditions: Ventricular Tachycardia deteriorating to Ventricular Fibrillation
explicitMissingInformation: Blood pressure (determine whether patient is stable or in cardiogenic shock)
History of prior MI, cardiomyopathy, or WPW
Serum potassium and toxicology exposure history

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: All regular wide-complex tachycardias must be clinically treated as Ventricular Tachycardia.

recommendedWorkup.action: Immediate 12-Lead ECG rhythm strip recording and continuous defibrillator pads placement
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Analyze AV dissociation and prepare for instant defibrillation/cardioversion.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Potassium, Magnesium, Calcium, Blood Gas, Troponin, and Tox Screen
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Rule out electrolyte triggers and toxic ingestion.

contradictionsAndCaveats: NEVER administer AV nodal blocking agents (Verapamil, Diltiazem, Adenosine, Beta-blockers) to an undifferentiated wide-complex tachycardia: in VT or WPW, calcium channel blockers precipitate catastrophic ventricular fibrillation and irreversible cardiac arrest!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: IF UNSTABLE (Syncope, dizziness, hypotension): Immediate Synchronized Electrical Cardioversion (100–200 Joules biphasic) with procedural sedation
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Instant restoration of organized rhythm and perfusion.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: IF STABLE: Pharmacologic cardioversion with IV Procainamide or IV Amiodarone
Cardiology / Electrophysiology (EP) Consultation and ICU admission

strictContraindications: Calcium channel blockers (Verapamil, Diltiazem) are ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in wide-complex tachycardia.
escalationTriggers: Loss of consciousness or pulse -> Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation (200J) and ACLS arrest protocol

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: ACLS Guidelines for Tachycardia with a Pulse

title: Question 11 – Acute ischemic stroke
vignette: 68-year-old female develops sudden right-sided weakness and expressive aphasia 75 minutes before arrival. BP 182/104 mmHg, glucose 118 mg/dL.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Ischemic Stroke (Left MCA / Large Vessel Occlusion)
top5Differentials.rationale: Sudden focal deficit (hemiparesis, expressive aphasia) within the time-critical 4.5h thrombolytic window.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Intracranial Hemorrhage (ICH)
top5Differentials.rationale: Clinically indistinguishable from ischemic stroke; mandates non-contrast CT rule-out prior to thrombolysis.

top5Differentials.name: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
top5Differentials.rationale: Transient focal ischemia; high impending stroke risk.

top5Differentials.name: Todd's Paresis post-Focal Seizure
top5Differentials.rationale: Postictal focal motor deficit; stroke mimic.

top5Differentials.name: Hypoglycemia (Stroke Mimic)
top5Differentials.rationale: Excluded by normal POC glucose 118 mg/dL.

explicitMissingInformation: Exact baseline NIHSS score
Medication history: DOACs (Apixaban, Rivaroxaban) or warfarin in past 48h
Recent surgery, head trauma, or bleeding history past 3 months

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Aphasia + hemiparesis predicts high likelihood of Large Vessel Occlusion (LVO).
Within golden window; pre-treatment BP < 185/110 mmHg.

recommendedWorkup.action: Non-Contrast Head CT (NCCT) within <= 20 minutes
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Rule out hemorrhage prior to thrombolysis.

recommendedWorkup.action: CT Angiography (CTA) of Head and Neck
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Detect LVO for emergent mechanical thrombectomy (EVT).

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat CBC (platelets), PT/INR, aPTT, Type & Screen
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Do NOT delay thrombolysis for labs unless coagulopathy suspected.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Permissive hypertension principle: In acute stroke, do NOT rapidly lower blood pressure! Target < 185/110 mmHg ONLY if giving thrombolysis. If not giving thrombolysis, allow BP up to 220/120 mmHg.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: CODE STROKE STAT ACTIVATION and emergent Non-Contrast Head CT <= 20 min
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Rule out ICH and establish reperfusion eligibility.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: IV Thrombolysis (Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg) if NCCT negative and BP < 185/110
Endovascular Mechanical Thrombectomy (EVT) if CTA confirms LVO

strictContraindications: Sublingual Nifedipine is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED (causes precipitate hypotension and stroke expansion).
Do NOT lower BP below 180/105 unless post-thrombolysis target.
escalationTriggers: CTA confirms LVO (M1 MCA or ICA terminus) -> Emergent neuro-interventional catheterization lab transfer

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Guidelines for Early Management of Patients with Acute Ischemic Stroke

title: Question 12 – Subarachnoid hemorrhage
vignette: 43-year-old male develops a sudden severe headache described as the worst headache of his life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds. He has neck stiffness and vomiting. CT performed four hours after onset is negative.

top5Differentials.name: Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH)
top5Differentials.rationale: Classic thunderclap headache peaking in seconds + meningismus + vomiting; CT false-negative rate exists.

top5Differentials.name: Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS)
top5Differentials.rationale: Recurrent thunderclap headaches with multifocal arterial constriction.

top5Differentials.name: Cervical / Vertebral Artery Dissection
top5Differentials.rationale: Sudden occipital/neck pain following minor trauma or spontaneous.

top5Differentials.name: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST)
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe headache with intracranial hypertension and vomiting.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Bacterial or Viral Meningitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe headache, neck stiffness, and vomiting; typically features fever.

explicitMissingInformation: Opening pressure on lumbar puncture
Visual acuity and fundoscopic exam for subhyaloid hemorrhages / papilledema
Blood pressure and neurological exam (focal cranial nerve III palsy)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Age >= 40, neck pain/stiffness, witnessed onset peaking within seconds, vomiting. Mandates complete investigation despite initial negative non-contrast CT.
Guides surgical/interventional aneurysm securing and ICU monitoring.

recommendedWorkup.action: Lumbar Puncture (LP) measuring opening pressure, cell counts in tubes 1 and 4, and spectrophotometric xanthochromia
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Definitive gold standard to detect xanthochromia when CT is negative.

recommendedWorkup.action: CT Angiography (CTA) of the Head and Neck
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Detect underlying berry aneurysm, vascular malformation, or dissection.

contradictionsAndCaveats: A negative CT at 4 hours has high sensitivity (~98-99%), but in high-suspicion presentations (meningismus, vomiting, thunderclap), standard consensus mandates Lumbar Puncture or CTA to definitively exclude an unruptured or micro-leaking aneurysm!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Strict Blood Pressure Control: IV Nicardipine or Labetalol targeting SBP < 140 mmHg
Initiate Nimodipine 60 mg PO/NG q4h
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Prevent secondary cerebral vasospasm and delayed ischemic deficits.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Emergent Neurosurgery and Neuro-interventional Consultation for aneurysm securing (coiling/clipping)

strictContraindications: NSAIDs and antiplatelets are STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED (increases fatal rebleeding risk).
Do NOT discharge patient with thunderclap headache and negative CT without LP or CTA vascular imaging.
escalationTriggers: Xanthochromia on LP or aneurysm demonstrated on CTA -> Emergent neurosurgical ICU admission

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Guidelines for the Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

title: Question 13 – Meningitis versus encephalitis
vignette: 19-year-old female presents with fever 39.4°C, headache, neck stiffness, confusion, and photophobia. HR 130 bpm.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Bacterial Meningitis (Neisseria meningitidis / S. pneumoniae)
top5Differentials.rationale: Classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status with high fever and tachycardia.

top5Differentials.name: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1) Encephalitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Prominent confusion, fever, and headache; temporal lobe necrosis if untreated.

top5Differentials.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage with Secondary Meningismus
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe headache and neck stiffness, though fever favors infectious etiology.

top5Differentials.name: Cerebral Malaria / Meningococcemia
top5Differentials.rationale: Fulminant sepsis with neurological obtundation and purpura.

top5Differentials.name: Brain Abscess with Elevated ICP
top5Differentials.rationale: Space-occupying infection; high herniation risk if LP performed blindly.

explicitMissingInformation: Blood pressure and respiratory rate (assess for septic shock and Cushing triad)
Skin exam: petechiae, purpura fulminans (meningococcal disease)
Focal neurological deficit or papilledema (determine LP safety before CT)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Altered mentation present; full sepsis screening required.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Blood Cultures x2 PRIOR to antibiotics (or immediately with first dose)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Identify causative pathogen without delaying therapy.

recommendedWorkup.action: Non-contrast Head CT BEFORE LP due to altered mental status (confusion)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Rule out space-occupying lesion or brain shift prior to dural puncture.

recommendedWorkup.action: Lumbar Puncture: CSF opening pressure, cell count, Gram stain, protein, glucose, bacterial antigens, and viral PCR (HSV)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Definitive CSF analysis following CT scan.

contradictionsAndCaveats: NEVER DELAY ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY FOR HEAD CT OR LUMBAR PUNCTURE: In suspected bacterial meningitis or encephalitis, draw blood cultures and administer IV antibiotics, dexamethasone, and acyclovir IMMEDIATELY before sending patient to CT!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: IMMEDIATE EMPIRIC ANTIMICROBIALS: IV Ceftriaxone 2g q12h + IV Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + IV Acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Sterilize CSF and prevent parenchymal necrosis.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: IV Dexamethasone 10 mg given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Reduce neurological morbidity, hearing loss, and mortality from pneumococcal meningitis.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Droplet isolation precautions and ICU admission
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Infection control for Neisseria meningitidis and intensive monitoring.

strictContraindications: Do NOT delay antibiotics to obtain a CT or lumbar puncture.
Do NOT perform LP in patients with focal neurological deficits, new seizures, or severe encephalopathy without a prior CT.
escalationTriggers: Rapid neurologic decline, purpuric rash spreading, or septic shock -> Intubation, ICU transfer

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis

title: Question 14 – Status epilepticus
vignette: 31-year-old male experiences continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizures lasting eight minutes without regaining consciousness. Oxygen saturation is 84%.

top5Differentials.name: Status Epilepticus (Early / Established)
top5Differentials.rationale: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting > 5 minutes without recovery of consciousness defines status epilepticus.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Hypoglycemic Seizure
top5Differentials.rationale: Profound neuroglycopenia triggering refractory seizures.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Intracranial Hemorrhage / SAH / Stroke
top5Differentials.rationale: Structural intracranial event precipitating acute seizures.

top5Differentials.name: Toxic Ingestion / Drug Toxicity (TCA, Isoniazid, Bupropion, Sympathomimetic)
top5Differentials.rationale: Toxin-induced lowering of seizure threshold.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Hyponatremia / Hypocalcemia
top5Differentials.rationale: Acute electrolyte shift producing cerebral edema and seizure.

explicitMissingInformation: Point-of-care capillary blood glucose (MANDATORY immediate bedside test)
Blood pressure, heart rate, temperature
History of epilepsy, antiepileptic drug compliance, or substance withdrawal

clinicalScores.scoreName: Neurocritical Care / AES Status Epilepticus Time Protocol
clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Seizure > 5 min warrants immediate first-line benzodiazepine therapy.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Point-of-Care Blood Glucose and Airway Positioning with High-Flow O2
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Treat hypoglycemia immediately and correct SpO2 84%.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Electrolytes (Na, Ca, Mg), Blood Gas, CBC, CMP, Anticonvulsant levels, Tox screen
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Identify metabolic and toxic precipitants.

recommendedWorkup.action: Continuous EEG Monitoring
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Detect non-convulsive status epilepticus following motor cessation.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Do NOT use neuromuscular blockers (Paralytics like Rocuronium or Succinylcholine) without continuous EEG or before antiepileptics: paralysis halts motor convulsions but brain electrographic status epilepticus continues, causing irreversible excitotoxic neuronal death!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: PHASE 1 (0–5 min): Airway support (bag-valve-mask with 100% O2) + POC Glucose check (give 50 mL D50W + Thiamine 100 mg if hypoglycemic)
PHASE 2 (5–20 min - First-Line Benzodiazepine): IV Lorazepam 4 mg IV push over 2 min (or IM Midazolam 10 mg if no IV access); repeat once at 5–10 min if seizure persists
PHASE 3 (20–40 min - Second-Line Urgent Antiepileptic): IV Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4500 mg) or IV Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg over 10-15 min
PHASE 4 (> 40 min - Refractory Status Epilepticus): Emergent endotracheal intubation and continuous anesthetic infusion (Propofol or Midazolam)

strictContraindications: Do NOT place tongue depressors or objects into the patient's mouth during active convulsions.
Do NOT delay second-line antiepileptics if benzodiazepines terminate the initial seizure.
escalationTriggers: Seizure continuous beyond 20 minutes -> Prepare for endotracheal intubation and continuous IV propofol

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Evidence-Based Guideline: Treatment of Convulsive Status Epilepticus in Children and Adults

title: Question 15 – Spinal cord compression
vignette: 59-year-old male with a history of prostate cancer presents with progressive lower back pain, bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, and urinary retention.

top5Differentials.name: Metastatic Epidural Spinal Cord Compression (MESCC)
top5Differentials.rationale: History of prostate cancer + back pain + bilateral motor weakness; oncologic surgical emergency.

top5Differentials.name: Cauda Equina Syndrome
top5Differentials.rationale: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, and bilateral leg weakness; requires surgical decompression within 24–48 hours to prevent permanent incontinence.

top5Differentials.name: Spinal Epidural Abscess / Spondylodiscitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Progressive neurologic deficit with back pain; infectious emergency.

top5Differentials.name: Spinal Epidural Hematoma
top5Differentials.rationale: Acute space-occupying compression.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Transverse Myelitis / Guillain-Barré Variant
top5Differentials.rationale: Bilateral weakness and autonomic dysfunction.

explicitMissingInformation: Post-void residual (PVR) volume (catheterization volume > 200–500 mL confirms neurogenic urinary retention)
Anal sphincter tone on digital rectal examination
Sensory level mapping to dermatome

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Preserved baseline motor function before intervention strongly predicts post-treatment ambulation.

recommendedWorkup.action: Emergent Whole-Spine MRI with and without IV contrast within <= 12–24 hours
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Gold standard to identify exact thecal sac compression and screen for multiple occult metastatic sites.

recommendedWorkup.action: Post-void catheterization and digital rectal examination
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Document neurogenic retention and anal sphincter tone.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Do NOT image only the lumbosacral spine: up to 30% of patients with metastatic spinal disease have multiple non-contiguous lesions. Whole-spine MRI is mandatory!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: High-Dose IV Corticosteroids: Dexamethasone 10–16 mg IV bolus immediately, then 4 mg IV q6h
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Reduce vasogenic spinal cord edema and preserve neuronal conduction.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Emergent Spine Neurosurgery and Radiation Oncology Consultations
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Mobilize for surgical decompression or urgent palliative radiotherapy.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Urinary Catheterization (Foley catheter placement)
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Relieve acute urinary retention and prevent permanent detrusor damage.

strictContraindications: Do NOT perform chiropractic spinal manipulation or physical therapy on suspected metastatic spine lesions.
Do NOT delay dexamethasone while waiting for the MRI scan.
escalationTriggers: Rapidly progressive motor deficit (inability to walk) -> Emergent OR for surgical decompression within hours

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Management of Metastatic Spinal Cord Compression

title: Question 16 – Sepsis with an unclear source
vignette: 45-year-old female presents with fever 39.5°C, HR 132 bpm, RR 28/min, BP 88/54 mmHg, and confusion. WBC 22,000/µL and lactate 4.6 mmol/L.

top5Differentials.name: Septic Shock / Sepsis-3 (Source Unclear)
top5Differentials.rationale: SIRS criteria met + hypotension (MAP 65.3) + lactate 4.6 + acute organ dysfunction (confusion, leukocytosis).

top5Differentials.name: Urosepsis / Acute Pyelonephritis
top5Differentials.rationale: Leading occult source of sepsis in adult females.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia / ARDS
top5Differentials.rationale: Tachypnea (RR 28) and tachycardia; frequent source of bacteremia.

top5Differentials.name: Intra-Abdominal Sepsis / Perforated Viscus
top5Differentials.rationale: Occult perforation or peritonitis producing profound lactic acidosis.

top5Differentials.name: Bacterial Meningitis / Meningococcemia
top5Differentials.rationale: High fever, tachycardia, and encephalopathy.

explicitMissingInformation: Arterial Blood Gas / PaO2 (assess lung injury and metabolic acid-base status)
Urine output / Foley catheter insertion
Source-specific physical exam (murmurs, peritoneal signs, costovertebral tenderness, skin lesions)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: RR >= 22 (+1), Altered Mentation (+1), SBP <= 100 (+1). Score 3/3 indicates severe risk of ICU admission and death. Note: qSOFA is NOT a diagnostic test for sepsis!
Suspected infection + organ dysfunction + refractory hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP >= 65 and lactate > 2 mmol/L.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Blood Cultures x2 sets PRIOR to antibiotics, Urinalysis & Urine culture, Sputum culture, Lactate remeasurement within 4 hours
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Hour-1 Sepsis Bundle components.

recommendedWorkup.action: Portable Chest Radiograph and POCUS Abdomen/Kidneys
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Identify source of occult infection.

recommendedWorkup.action: Invasive Arterial Line and Central Venous Access
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Titrate vasopressors and monitor volume responsiveness.

contradictionsAndCaveats: qSOFA is a PROGNOSTIC score for mortality risk, NOT a diagnostic score for sepsis: a qSOFA < 2 does NOT rule out sepsis!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: HOUR-1 SEPSIS BUNDLE - Fluid Resuscitation: Rapid IV infusion of 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid (Lactated Ringer's) within 3 hours
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Restore intravascular volume and stroke volume.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: HOUR-1 SEPSIS BUNDLE - Blood Cultures and Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics: IV Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + IV Cefepime 2g (or Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g)
HOUR-1 SEPSIS BUNDLE - Vasopressor Therapy: Norepinephrine infusion titrated to maintain MAP >= 65 mmHg if hypotension persists during/after fluid load

strictContraindications: Do NOT delay broad-spectrum antibiotics beyond 1 hour for diagnostic tests or culture collection in septic shock.
Do NOT administer Dopamine as first-line vasopressor (Norepinephrine is superior with lower tachyarrhythmia risk).
escalationTriggers: Persistent hypotension requiring high-dose norepinephrine -> Add Vasopressin 0.03 units/min + Stress-dose hydrocortisone

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock

title: Question 17 – Necrotizing fasciitis
vignette: 52-year-old diabetic male presents with severe thigh pain, fever, and swelling. Temperature 39°C, HR 125 bpm. Skin changes appear relatively mild despite severe pain. Sodium 129 mmol/L, CRP 240 mg/L, WBC 21,000/µL.

top5Differentials.name: Necrotizing Fasciitis (Type I Polymicrobial vs Type II Monomicrobial GAS)
top5Differentials.rationale: Pain out of proportion to physical exam + systemic toxicity + severe laboratory abnormalities in diabetic male.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Cellulitis / Erysipelas
top5Differentials.rationale: Superficial soft tissue infection; does NOT account for profound pain out of proportion or severe hyponatremia/SIRS.

top5Differentials.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis with Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe thigh pain and swelling; lacks early skin changes.

top5Differentials.name: Pyomyositis / Deep Intramuscular Abscess
top5Differentials.rationale: Deep muscle suppuration in immunocompromised/diabetic patient.

top5Differentials.name: Compartment Syndrome of the Thigh
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe pain on passive stretch with swelling.

explicitMissingInformation: Hemoglobin, Serum Glucose, and Serum Creatinine (to calculate complete LRINEC score)
Crepitus on palpation, bullae, skin anesthesia, or dishwater fluid exudate
Blood pressure (assess for septic shock)

clinicalScores.scoreName: LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis)
clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: CRP >= 150 (+4), WBC 15-25 (+1), Sodium < 135 (+2). Score >= 6 indicates high risk. CRITICAL LIMITATION: LRINEC has poor sensitivity (~68-80%); a low score NEVER safely rules out necrotizing fasciitis!

recommendedWorkup.action: IMMEDIATE SURGICAL BEDSIDE EVALUATION & EXPLORATION (Finger test / operative exploration)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Definitive diagnosis is exclusively surgical; do not delay for imaging!

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Blood Cultures x2, Lactate, CMP, CBC, Creatine Kinase (CK)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Assess myonecrosis and multi-organ dysfunction.

recommendedWorkup.action: Bedside Ultrasound (POCUS) to screen for subcutaneous fluid/air while awaiting OR
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Radiographic air is specific but only present in ~30%.

contradictionsAndCaveats: A benign-appearing skin examination NEVER excludes necrotizing fasciitis: the infection spreads along deep fascial planes beneath intact skin. PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION is the hallmark warning sign!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: STAT EMERGENCY SURGICAL CONSULTATION FOR OPERATIVE DEBRIDEMENT
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Life-saving wide surgical excision of necrotic fascia.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Broad-Spectrum Triple IV Antibiotic Regimen: IV Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + IV Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g + IV Clindamycin 900 mg q8h
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Cover MRSA, Gram-negatives, and suppress toxin production (Clindamycin antitoxin effect).

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Aggressive IV Fluid Resuscitation and ICU Bed Reservation
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Treat septic shock and tissue hypoperfusion.

strictContraindications: Do NOT delay emergency surgical debridement to obtain CT or MRI imaging.
Do NOT rely on a low LRINEC score to rule out necrotizing infection.
escalationTriggers: Skin bullae, crepitus, purple discoloration, or septic shock -> Immediate transport to Operating Room

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Guidelines for the Management of Severe Skin and Soft-Tissue Infections

title: Question 18 – Infective endocarditis
vignette: 41-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fever, night sweats, fatigue, and a new systolic murmur. Blood cultures show gram-positive cocci.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Infective Endocarditis (Tricuspid vs Aortic/Mitral)
top5Differentials.rationale: IVDU + fever + new systolic murmur + gram-positive bacteremia is diagnostic for IE until proven otherwise.

top5Differentials.name: Septic Pulmonary Emboli secondary to Right-Sided Endocarditis
top5Differentials.rationale: Tricuspid vegetations fragmenting into pulmonary circulation.

top5Differentials.name: Catheter-Related / Deep Venous Suppurative Thrombophlebitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Infected vein thrombophlebitis from non-sterile vascular access.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Pericarditis / Myocardial Abscess
top5Differentials.rationale: Annular extension of endocarditis causing heart block.

top5Differentials.name: Occult Epidural Abscess or Vertebral Osteomyelitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Metastatic septic seeding of the spine from bacteremia.

mustNotMissConditions: Acute Aortic / Mitral Valve Destruction with Acute Heart Failure
Perivalvular Ring Abscess with Heart Block
explicitMissingInformation: Identified species of Gram-positive cocci (Staphylococcus aureus vs Enterococcus vs Streptococcus)
12-lead ECG (evaluate for new 1st-degree AV block indicating aortic ring abscess)
Stigmata of IE on physical exam (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, splinter hemorrhages, Roth spots)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Major criterion 1 (bacteremia) + Major criterion 2 (new regurgitant murmur) + Minor criteria (IVDU, fever). Fulfills definite IE criteria.

recommendedWorkup.action: Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE) followed immediately by Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: TEE has > 90-95% sensitivity to detect vegetations, ring abscess, and valve perforation.

recommendedWorkup.action: Serial Blood Cultures (3 sets from separate venipuncture sites spaced at least 30-60 min apart)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Document persistent bacteremia and antimicrobial susceptibility.

recommendedWorkup.action: Daily 12-lead ECG monitoring
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Detect PR prolongation indicating perivalvular aortic root extension.

contradictionsAndCaveats: A negative Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE) NEVER excludes endocarditis (TTE misses up to 40-50% of vegetations, especially in prosthetic valves or small vegetations). TEE is mandatory in high-risk patients!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Empiric Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics: IV Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg q8-12h + IV Cefepime 2g (to cover MRSA, Enterococcus, and Gram-negative bacilli)
Emergent Cardiothoracic Surgery Consultation
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Evaluate indications for urgent surgical valve replacement.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Telemetry and daily ECG monitoring
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Monitor for conduction block and ventricular arrhythmias.

strictContraindications: Do NOT initiate anticoagulation in native-valve endocarditis (significantly increases risk of fatal hemorrhagic stroke from mycotic aneurysms).
Do NOT rely on TTE alone to rule out endocarditis.
escalationTriggers: New heart block, acute severe pulmonary edema/heart failure, or vegetation > 10 mm -> Emergent cardiac surgery

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Infective Endocarditis in Adults: Diagnosis, Antimicrobial Therapy, and Management of Complications

title: Question 19 – Severe malaria
vignette: 29-year-old male recently returned from Ghana presents with fever, chills, confusion, jaundice, and dark urine. Platelets 48,000/µL, hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, and elevated bilirubin.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Plasmodium falciparum Malaria (Cerebral Malaria & Hemoglobinuria)
top5Differentials.rationale: Travel to endemic region + fever + cerebral involvement (confusion) + hemolysis (anemia, jaundice, blackwater urine) + thrombocytopenia.

top5Differentials.name: Fulminant Sepsis / Meningococcemia
top5Differentials.rationale: High fever, confusion, and consumptive coagulopathy.

top5Differentials.name: Yellow Fever / Viral Hemorrhagic Fever (Lassa)
top5Differentials.rationale: Endemic West African viral infection with hepatitis, jaundice, and coagulopathy.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Viral Hepatitis with Hepatic Encephalopathy
top5Differentials.rationale: Jaundice and confusion; lacks severe thrombocytopenia and acute hemolysis.

top5Differentials.name: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)
top5Differentials.rationale: Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, and confusion.

mustNotMissConditions: Severe Blackwater Fever Hemolysis with Acute Renal Failure
explicitMissingInformation: Exact percentage parasitemia on peripheral thin blood smear
Serum Creatinine and Lactate (WHO criteria for severe malaria)
Blood glucose (severe malaria induces profound hypoglycemia)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Impaired consciousness (cerebral malaria) + Jaundice + Severe anemia + Hemoglobinuria. Mortality > 20%; mandates immediate IV artesunate.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Giemsa-stained Thick and Thin Peripheral Blood Smears with quantitative parasitemia calculation
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Definitive gold standard to identify species (P. falciparum) and quantify parasite burden.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat Malaria Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT for Pf-HRP2) and POC Blood Glucose
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Immediate confirmation while smears are processed.

recommendedWorkup.action: CMP (Cr, Bilirubin, AST/ALT), Blood Gas/Lactate, Urinalysis (hemoglobinuria)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Assess acute kidney injury and lactic acidosis.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Oral antimalarial therapy (Coartem) is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in severe malaria: impaired oral intake, vomiting, and organ failure mandate parenteral IV therapy!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: FIRST-LINE ANTIMALARIAL: IV Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg IV immediately at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then daily
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Rapid parasite clearance (superior mortality reduction vs quinine).

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Check and treat hypoglycemia (POC glucose < 60 mg/dL with IV D50W)
Cautious fluid management and ICU admission
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Avoid aggressive overhydration (high risk of non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS).

strictContraindications: Do NOT administer oral antimalarials in severe malaria.
Do NOT over-resuscitate with fluids (ARDS is a leading cause of death in severe malaria).
escalationTriggers: Parasitemia > 10%, respiratory distress (ARDS), or oliguric acute renal failure -> Hemodialysis, mechanical ventilation

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Guidelines for the Treatment of Malaria (3rd edition)

title: Question 20 – Hospital-acquired infection
vignette: 73-year-old female develops fever, hypotension, and worsening respiratory distress on day six of hospitalization. She has a central venous catheter and urinary catheter.

top5Differentials.name: Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia / VAP
top5Differentials.rationale: New respiratory distress and fever after > 48h hospitalization; high risk for Pseudomonas and MRSA.

top5Differentials.name: Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI)
top5Differentials.rationale: Indwelling CVC with abrupt fever and septic hypotension.

top5Differentials.name: Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI) with Urosepsis
top5Differentials.rationale: Foley catheter colonization progressing to bacteremia.

top5Differentials.name: Hospital-Acquired Acute Pulmonary Embolism
top5Differentials.rationale: Sudden respiratory distress and hypotension in hospitalized bedridden patient.

top5Differentials.name: Clostridioides difficile Colitis with Toxic Megacolon
top5Differentials.rationale: Hospital-acquired nosocomial infection with systemic sepsis.

explicitMissingInformation: Chest radiograph comparison with baseline (new infiltrate/consolidation)
PaO2/FiO2 ratio and ventilator settings
Physical exam of CVC insertion site (erythema, purulence, induration)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Hospital-acquired sepsis with hypotension and organ failure.

recommendedWorkup.action: Paired Blood Cultures: 1 set from CVC lumen + 1 set from peripheral venipuncture
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Calculate differential time to positivity to confirm CLABSI.

recommendedWorkup.action: Endotracheal aspirate / Sputum culture, Urinalysis & Urine culture, Lactate
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Isolate nosocomial respiratory and urinary pathogens.

recommendedWorkup.action: Portable Chest Radiograph and bedside echocardiogram
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Evaluate new lung consolidation and line tip position.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Standard community-acquired antibiotic regimens (Ceftriaxone, Ampicillin) are STRICTLY INSUFFICIENT for nosocomial day-6 sepsis: empiric coverage MUST cover resistant pathogens (MRSA + Pseudomonas aeruginosa)!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Empiric Broad-Spectrum Nosocomial Sepsis Coverage: IV Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + IV Cefepime 2g q8h (or Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g q6h or Meropenem 1g q8h)
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Cover MRSA, Pseudomonas, and MDR enteric bacilli.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg) and Norepinephrine infusion for MAP >= 65 mmHg
Remove/exchange indwelling central venous catheter and replace Foley catheter

strictContraindications: Do NOT delay antibiotics for catheter exchange or imaging.
escalationTriggers: Severe hypoxemia PaO2/FiO2 < 200 or refractory shock -> Transfer to Intensive Care Unit

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Management of Hospital-Acquired and Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia

title: Question 21 – Severe asthma exacerbation
vignette: 24-year-old female with asthma presents with severe breathlessness, inability to complete sentences, RR 34/min, HR 140 bpm, and oxygen saturation 88%. Peak expiratory flow is 28% of predicted.

top5Differentials.name: Severe / Life-Threatening Asthma Exacerbation (Status Asthmaticus)
top5Differentials.rationale: PEF < 30%, tachypnea (RR 34), tachycardia (HR 140), hypoxia (88%), and inability to complete sentences.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax
top5Differentials.rationale: Airway barotrauma and bullous rupture in severe bronchospasm.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Anaphylaxis with Bronchospasm
top5Differentials.rationale: Sudden severe respiratory distress, wheezing, and tachycardia.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Pulmonary Embolism
top5Differentials.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, hypoxemia, and tachycardia.

top5Differentials.name: Foreign Body Aspiration / Laryngeal Edema
top5Differentials.rationale: Upper airway obstruction mimicking bronchospasm.

explicitMissingInformation: Arterial Blood Gas (PaCO2: normal or elevated PaCO2 >= 42 mmHg indicates impending respiratory failure)
Pneumothorax signs on auscultation (unilateral absent breath sounds)
Use of accessory muscles / silent chest

clinicalScores.scoreName: GINA Severity Assessment for Acute Asthma
clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: PEF < 50%, RR > 30, HR > 120, SpO2 < 90%, words in phrases. High risk of fatal arrest; warrants ICU admission.

recommendedWorkup.action: Continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac telemetry, and serial PEF measurements
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Assess response to bronchodilators.

recommendedWorkup.action: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) if not rapidly responding
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Detect hypercapnia and respiratory fatigue.

recommendedWorkup.action: Portable Chest Radiograph
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Rule out pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, and pneumonia.

contradictionsAndCaveats: A 'normal' PaCO2 (38-42 mmHg) in a severely tachypneic asthmatic (RR 34) is NOT reassuring: it is an OMINOUS SIGN of respiratory muscle exhaustion and impending catastrophic arrest (pseudonormalization)!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: High-Flow Oxygen targeting SpO2 93–95%
Continuous Nebulized SABA + SAMA: Albuterol 5 mg + Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized continuously or q20 min x 3 doses
Systemic Corticosteroids: IV Methylprednisolone 60 mg or PO Prednisone 50 mg immediately
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Inhibit airway inflammation and upregulate beta receptors.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: IV Magnesium Sulfate 2g IV infusion over 20 minutes
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Direct bronchial smooth muscle relaxation in refractory severe asthma.

strictContraindications: Sedatives and hypnotics (benzodiazepines) are STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED (depresses respiratory drive and precipitates fatal arrest).
Do NOT delay bronchodilators or steroids for diagnostic imaging.
escalationTriggers: Silent chest, worsening PaCO2 > 42 mmHg, confusion -> Emergent RSI with Ketamine and ICU admission

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention

title: Question 22 – COPD exacerbation with respiratory failure
vignette: 70-year-old male with COPD presents with worsening breathlessness and confusion. ABG: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 78 mmHg, PaO₂ 54 mmHg, HCO₃ 33 mmol/L.

top5Differentials.name: Acute-on-Chronic Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure (COPD Exacerbation)
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe respiratory acidosis (pH 7.25, PaCO2 78) with metabolic compensation (HCO3 33) and encephalopathy.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Pulmonary Embolism in COPD
top5Differentials.rationale: Trigger of refractory hypoxemia in COPD.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Community-Acquired / Nosocomial Pneumonia
top5Differentials.rationale: Common precipitant of acute hypercapnic decompensation.

top5Differentials.name: Pneumothorax (Secondary Spontaneous)
top5Differentials.rationale: Rupture of emphysematous bulla triggering acute decompensation.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Congestive Heart Failure / Cor Pulmonale Decompensation
top5Differentials.rationale: Right/left ventricular failure exacerbating dyspnea.

explicitMissingInformation: Current inspired oxygen concentration (FiO2: evaluate for oxygen-induced hypercapnia)
Sputum volume, purulence, and fever (Anthonisen criteria)
Baseline ABG or PaCO2

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: High PaCO2 (78) with uncompensated low pH (7.25) despite elevated chronic HCO3 (33). Fulfills criteria for urgent Non-Invasive Ventilation.

recommendedWorkup.action: Continuous pulse oximetry, ABG repeat at 1-2 hours, and telemetry
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Monitor response to ventilatory support.

recommendedWorkup.action: Portable Chest Radiograph
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Rule out pneumonia, pneumothorax, and cardiomegaly.

recommendedWorkup.action: CBC, CMP, BNP, Sputum culture, Blood cultures if febrile
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Identify infectious precipitant and heart failure.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Do NOT deliver uncontrolled high-flow oxygen (100% NRB): targeting SpO2 100% in chronic hypercapnic COPD worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch and the Haldane effect, triggering lethal CO2 narcosis and coma! TARGET SpO2 88–92%!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: FIRST-LINE VENTILATORY SUPPORT: Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (BiPAP: IPAP 10-12 cmH2O, EPAP 4-5 cmH2O)
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Reduce work of breathing, blow off CO2, and avoid invasive intubation (reduces mortality > 50%).

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Controlled Oxygen Therapy: Titrate Venturi mask or nasal cannula to strict SpO2 target of 88–92%
Inhaled Bronchodilators (Albuterol + Ipratropium) and Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisone 40 mg PO or IV Methylprednisolone 40 mg)

strictContraindications: Hyperoxia (SpO2 > 96%) is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in acute hypercapnic COPD.
Respiratory depressants (opioids, sedatives) are contraindicated.
escalationTriggers: Worsening pH < 7.20, worsening encephalopathy, or inability to protect airway on BiPAP -> Endotracheal intubation

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Global Strategy for Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of COPD

title: Question 23 – Tension pneumothorax
vignette: 35-year-old male presents following a motor vehicle collision with severe respiratory distress, hypotension, absent breath sounds on the right, and distended neck veins.

top5Differentials.name: Tension Pneumothorax (Right-Sided)
top5Differentials.rationale: Trauma + severe respiratory distress + hypotension (obstructive shock) + absent right breath sounds + JVD (vena cava compression).

top5Differentials.name: Cardiac Tamponade (Traumatic Hemopericardium)
top5Differentials.rationale: Hypotension and JVD (Beck's triad); breath sounds are typically equal bilaterally.

top5Differentials.name: Massive Hemothorax
top5Differentials.rationale: Absent breath sounds and shock post-MVC; neck veins are usually flat due to hypovolemia.

top5Differentials.name: Tracheobronchial Tree Disruption
top5Differentials.rationale: Massive air leak post-blunt thoracic trauma.

top5Differentials.name: Traumatic Diaphragmatic Rupture with Visceral Herniation
top5Differentials.rationale: Abdominal viscera entering hemithorax causing lung collapse.

explicitMissingInformation: Numeric blood pressure and heart rate (quantify obstructive shock)
Tracheal deviation (late clinical sign)
Associated injuries (pelvic fracture, head trauma)

clinicalScores.scoreName: ATLS Trauma Triage (Advanced Trauma Life Support)
clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Pure clinical diagnosis; mandates instant needle or finger thoracostomy.

recommendedWorkup.action: IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY THORACIC DECOMPRESSION (DO NOT OBTAIN X-RAY PRIOR TO INTERVENTION)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a PURE CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS. Delaying decompression for CXR is fatal!

recommendedWorkup.action: eFAST Exam (Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Evaluate lung sliding and rule out pericardial tamponade in seconds.

contradictionsAndCaveats: NEVER DELAY EMERGENCY DECOMPRESSION FOR A CHEST RADIOGRAPH OR CT SCAN: Waiting for imaging in tension pneumothorax results in complete cardiac arrest from inferior vena cava collapse and obstructive shock!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: IMMEDIATE DECOMPRESSION: Emergent Needle Thoracostomy (14G 3.25-inch catheter in 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line or 4th/5th intercostal space anterior axillary line) or Finger Thoracostomy
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Convert tension pneumothorax to simple open pneumothorax and restore venous return.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Tube Thoracostomy (Chest Tube, 28–32 Fr) in the 5th intercostal space mid-to-anterior axillary line
Post-decompression Chest Radiograph and Trauma Team Activation
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Confirm tube position and rule out persistent hemothorax.

strictContraindications: Do NOT send a hemodynamically unstable trauma patient with absent unilateral breath sounds to the CT scanner or for a formal X-ray.
Do NOT remove chest tube without confirmation of seal and resolution.
escalationTriggers: Chest tube output > 1500 mL initially or > 200 mL/hr for 2-4 hours -> Emergent thoracotomy / OR transfer

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: ATLS: Advanced Trauma Life Support (10th edition)

title: Question 24 – Diabetic ketoacidosis
vignette: 28-year-old female with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep rapid breathing. Glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.12, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, anion gap 26, potassium 5.6 mmol/L.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
top5Differentials.rationale: High glucose (480) + metabolic acidosis (pH 7.12, HCO3 8) + severe anion gap (26) + Kussmaul respirations in T1D.

top5Differentials.name: Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS) / Mixed DKA-HHS
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe hyperglycemia with dehydration; acidemia confirms dominant DKA.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Surgical Abdomen / Appendicitis / Perforation
top5Differentials.rationale: Abdominal pain is common in DKA, but intra-abdominal sepsis can trigger DKA.

top5Differentials.name: Toxic Ingestion (Methanol, Ethylene Glycol, Salicylate Toxicity)
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis with hyperventilation.

top5Differentials.name: Alcoholic Ketoacidosis (AKA)
top5Differentials.rationale: Ketoacidosis with vomiting; usually features normal or low glucose.

explicitMissingInformation: Serum Sodium (calculate corrected sodium and effective osmolality)
Urine/Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate level
Precipitating factor: infection (WBC, cultures), missed insulin, myocardial ischemia

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: pH < 7.20 (7.12), HCO3 < 10 (8), Anion Gap > 12 (26). High mortality; requires ICU admission and continuous IV regular insulin.
Potassium > 5.2 mEq/L: Safe to initiate insulin. Withhold IV KCl until K+ drops < 5.2.

recommendedWorkup.action: Basic Metabolic Panel, Venous Blood Gas, Serum Beta-hydroxybutyrate, Urinalysis, CBC
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Serial monitoring of anion gap, potassium, and acidosis q2-4 hours.

recommendedWorkup.action: Blood cultures, Chest X-ray, 12-lead ECG
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Identify precipitating infection or myocardial infarction.

contradictionsAndCaveats: NEVER start insulin if Serum Potassium is < 3.3 mEq/L: insulin drives potassium into cells, triggering fatal hypokalemic cardiac arrhythmias! Correct potassium first!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: FLUID RESUSCITATION FIRST: 0.9% Normal Saline 1,000–1,500 mL IV over the first hour
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Restore effective circulating volume and renal perfusion.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: CONTINUOUS IV INSULIN: IV Regular Insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hr (target glucose decrease 50–75 mg/dL/hr)
DEXTROSE TRANSITION: When glucose reaches 200–250 mg/dL, add 5% Dextrose to IV fluids (D5 0.45% NS)
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Prevent hypoglycemia while continuing insulin until anion gap closes (HCO3 >= 18, pH > 7.30, AG <= 12).

strictContraindications: Do NOT stop insulin when blood glucose drops to 200 mg/dL: add dextrose and continue insulin to clear ketoacidosis!
Do NOT administer routine IV sodium bicarbonate unless pH < 6.9 (worsens intracellular acidosis and causes hypokalemia).
escalationTriggers: Development of headache, lethargy, or bradycardia -> Suspect Cerebral Edema -> IV Mannitol or 3% Hypertonic Saline

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Management of Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults

title: Question 25 – Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
vignette: 76-year-old male presents with confusion, severe dehydration, and weakness. Glucose 920 mg/dL, sodium 148 mmol/L, BUN 48 mg/dL.

top5Differentials.name: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
top5Differentials.rationale: Extreme hyperglycemia (920), hyperosmolality (> 340), severe dehydration (BUN 48), and encephalopathy in elderly patient.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Ischemic Stroke with Stress Hyperglycemia
top5Differentials.rationale: Focal or global neurologic deficit in elderly diabetic.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Sepsis / Urosepsis / Pneumonia triggering HHS
top5Differentials.rationale: Leading infectious precipitant of HHS.

top5Differentials.name: Mixed DKA-HHS
top5Differentials.rationale: Features of both severe hyperosmolality and metabolic acidosis.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Kidney Injury / Prerenal Azotemia
top5Differentials.rationale: Dehydration-induced renal failure.

mustNotMissConditions: Osmotic Cerebral Edema from Rapid Glucose Drops
explicitMissingInformation: Serum Potassium, Bicarbonate, and Blood Gas (confirm absence of significant ketoacidosis)
Serum Creatinine (calculate fluid deficit)
Precipitating cause (urinary/chest infection, stroke, MI)

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: 2(Na) + Glucose/18 = 2(148) + 920/18 = 347.1 mOsm/kg. Well above diagnostic threshold (> 320 mOsm/kg). Confirms HHS.

recommendedWorkup.action: BMP, Blood Gas, Lactate, Urinalysis, Serum Osmolality, Blood cultures
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Confirm absence of acidosis and identify infection.

recommendedWorkup.action: Non-Contrast Head CT and Chest X-ray
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Rule out acute intracranial event and pneumonia.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Do NOT lower blood glucose too rapidly in HHS (> 75–100 mg/dL/hr): rapid drops in extracellular osmolality cause dangerous osmotic fluid shifts into the central nervous system, producing fatal cerebral edema!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: AGGRESSIVE FLUID REHYDRATION (PRIMARY THERAPY): 1,000–1,500 mL 0.9% Normal Saline in the first hour, then 0.45% NS if corrected sodium is normal/high
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Restore vascular volume and expand GFR (fluid deficit is typically 8–10 Liters).

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Cautious IV Regular Insulin infusion (0.05–0.1 units/kg/hr) STARTED ONLY AFTER INITIAL FLUID EXPANSION
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Gradual lowering of glucose (target drop 50-75 mg/dL/hr).

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Prophylactic anticoagulation with LMWH
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Prevent venous thromboembolism (severe hyperosmolality induces hyperviscosity and thrombosis).

strictContraindications: Do NOT start insulin before adequate initial fluid resuscitation (insulin without fluids drives glucose and water into cells, worsening hypovolemic vascular collapse).
Avoid hypotonic fluids initially.
escalationTriggers: Deterioration in mental status or hemodynamic shock -> ICU admission

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults with Diabetes

title: Question 26 – Adrenal crisis
vignette: 46-year-old female with a history of long-term corticosteroid use presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, and hypotension. Sodium 124 mmol/L, potassium 6.1 mmol/L, glucose 52 mg/dL.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Adrenal Crisis (Secondary to HPA-Axis Suppression)
top5Differentials.rationale: Steroid history + refractory hypotension + hyponatremia (124) + hyperkalemia (6.1) + hypoglycemia (52).

top5Differentials.name: Septic Shock with Relative Adrenal Insufficiency
top5Differentials.rationale: Hypotension and vomiting precipitated by occult infection.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Surgical Abdomen / Peritonitis
top5Differentials.rationale: Severe abdominal pain and vomiting mimicking surgical abdomen.

top5Differentials.name: Primary Addisonian Crisis (Autoimmune Adrenalitis)
top5Differentials.rationale: Mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Toxic Overdose / Digoxin or Beta-blocker Toxicity
top5Differentials.rationale: Hypotension and hyperkalemia.

mustNotMissConditions: Acute Adrenal Crisis / Refractory Cardiovascular Collapse
explicitMissingInformation: Exact blood pressure and heart rate (fluid-refractory hypotension)
12-lead ECG (evaluate peaked T waves from K+ 6.1)
Precipitating illness: infection, trauma, surgery, or abrupt steroid cessation

clinicalScores.scoreName: Diagnostic Electrolyte Tetrad for Adrenal Crisis
clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Loss of cortisol permissiveness causes catecholamine-resistant vascular collapse; mandates instant steroid replacement.

recommendedWorkup.action: Draw stat Random Cortisol and ACTH level PRIOR to steroid administration (DO NOT WAIT FOR RESULTS)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Document baseline adrenal failure.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat 12-lead ECG and POC Glucose verification
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Assess hyperkalemic cardiotoxicity and treat hypoglycemia.

contradictionsAndCaveats: NEVER WAIT FOR CORTISOL OR ACTH TEST RESULTS TO INITIATE TREATMENT: Adrenal crisis is fatal within hours from circulatory collapse. Administer IV hydrocortisone immediately!

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: IMMEDIATE STEROID REPLACEMENT: IV Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV push immediately, then 50–100 mg IV q6h
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Restore vascular tone and glucocorticoid activity.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: GLUCOSE AND VOLUME RESUSCITATION: IV 5% Dextrose in 0.9% Normal Saline (D5NS) 1,000 mL bolus
immediateManagementPlan.objective: Simultaneously treat hypotension, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia.

immediateManagementPlan.intervention: Treat hyperkalemia (K+ 6.1) with IV Calcium Gluconate if ECG changes present

strictContraindications: Do NOT delay corticosteroid therapy for diagnostic laboratory results.
Do NOT give pure hypotonic fluids (D5W alone) without normal saline.
escalationTriggers: Hypotension refractory to fluids and hydrocortisone -> Vasopressor support (Norepinephrine) in ICU

guidelineCitations.guidelineName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

title: Question 27 – Acute kidney injury
vignette: 64-year-old male presents with reduced urine output, confusion, and generalized weakness. Creatinine increased from 1.0 to 3.8 mg/dL within 48 hours. Potassium 6.8 mmol/L, ECG shows peaked T waves.

top5Differentials.name: Severe Hyperkalemic Emergency secondary to KDIGO Stage 3 AKI
top5Differentials.rationale: Creatinine rise > 3x baseline within 48h + K+ 6.8 with cardiotoxicity (peaked T waves); impending sine wave and asystole.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Obstructive Uropathy (Post-Renal AKI / BPH / Malignancy)
top5Differentials.rationale: Abrupt oliguria in older male; reversible with urgent decompression.

top5Differentials.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN - Ischemic or Nephrotoxic)
top5Differentials.rationale: Intrinsic renal failure from hypoperfusion or medications.

top5Differentials.name: Rhabdomyolysis-Induced AKI
top5Differentials.rationale: Weakness and myoglobinuria causing acute renal shutdown and hyperkalemia.

top5Differentials.name: Uremic Encephalopathy / Uremic Pericarditis
top5Differentials.rationale: Confusion and azotemia indicating severe uremic toxicity.

explicitMissingInformation: Bedside bladder scan volume / post-void residual
Urine output rate (mL/kg/hr)
Medication history: ACEi, ARB, Spironolactone, NSAIDs, Trimethoprim

clinicalScores.clinicalMeaning: Serum creatinine increase >= 3.0 times baseline (1.0 -> 3.8 mg/dL). High risk of mortality and urgent dialysis indication.

recommendedWorkup.action: CONTINUOUS CARDIAC TELEMETRY and repeat 12-lead ECG q15-30 min
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Monitor for sine-wave deterioration and response to calcium.

recommendedWorkup.action: Bedside Bladder Scan and Renal Ultrasound (POCUS)
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Rule out bilateral hydronephrosis / urinary outflow obstruction.

recommendedWorkup.action: Stat BMP, Calcium, Blood Gas (acidosis), Creatine Kinase, Urinalysis
recommendedWorkup.rationale: Assess acidemia, hypocalcemia, and rhabdomyolysis.

contradictionsAndCaveats: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate) is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in the acute management of hyperkalemic emergency: it has delayed onset (hours) and causes bowel necrosis. Membrane stabilization with Calcium is the absolute immediate priority!
